summary: This RFC is the official specification of the Hostname Server Protocol, a service for fetching host table information from a server. It revises RFC 811 and is historic.

eli5.summary: You ask a computer to look in its list of computer names and tell you what you want to know.

questions: what is the hostname server protocol
how to get the host table from a server
what port does the hostname server use
what are the hostname server error codes
subtitle: A one-question-per-connection service for fetching the Internet host table over TCP.

tldr.problem: Programs on the early Internet needed a machine-readable way to get name and address information about networks, gateways and hosts from the central Network Information Center.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a TCP connection to port 101 on SRI-NIC.ARPA, sends one line such as HNAME or ALL, reads the response, and the server closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: RFC 953 is marked Historic; it revised RFC 811 and pointed toward the Domain Name System as the future.

today: RFC 953 has Historic status. It obsoletes RFC 811 and has not been obsoleted by a later RFC.

sections.title: What the Hostname Server Does
sections.content:
The NIC Internet Hostname Server is a TCP-based host information program and protocol that ran on the SRI-NIC machine. It was one of a series of Internet name services kept by the DDN Network Information Center (NIC) at SRI International.

Its job is to deliver machine-readable name and address information describing networks, gateways, hosts and eventually domains. As implemented, it provides the information described in the DoD Internet Host Table Specification (RFC 952). This memo is the official specification of the protocol and includes minor revisions to RFC 811, which it obsoletes. It also points to RFC 921 for the future Domain Name System.
sections.eli5: There was one computer that kept the official list of every computer's name and number. This service let other computers ask it for entries from that list.

sections.title: Connecting and Asking
sections.content:
To use the server, a program opens a TCP connection to port 101 (decimal) at the service host, SRI-NIC.ARPA (26.0.0.73 or 10.0.0.51). It sends the information request as a single line and reads the response. The server closes the connection when the response is complete, so only one request can be made per connection.

A request has the form <command key> <argument(s)> [<options>]. A response has the form <response key> : <rest of response>. A response may run over several lines; continuation lines always begin with at least one space.

The RFC warns clients to check what kind of reply they got. An ALL request will likely return several hundred or more records, while HNAME or HADDR will usually return one HOST record.
sections.eli5: You dial in, ask exactly one question on a single line, listen to the answer, and the line goes dead. If you have another question, you dial again.

sections.title: Commands and Response Keys
sections.content:
The commands include HELP, VERSION, HNAME (look up by host name), HADDR (look up by host address), ALL (the entire host table), ALL-OLD, DOMAINS, ALL-DOM and ALL-INGWAY. Because the server and its features would evolve, the RFC says to use HELP for the most recent summary.

VERSION lets an automated process check whether a new version of the host table exists without transferring the whole table. The version string is only guaranteed to be unique to each version, and nothing should be assumed about its format.

Response keys are ERR, NET, GATEWAY, HOST, DOMAIN, BEGIN and END. For example, HNAME SRI-NIC.ARPA is likely answered by a HOST record listing the addresses, names, machine type, operating system and services. An ALL request gets BEGIN, then the table in the RFC 952 format, then END:.
sections.eli5: There is a short menu of words you can say, like ask-by-name, ask-by-number, or give-me-everything. The answer starts with a word that says what kind of answer it is.

sections.title: Error Replies
sections.content:
An ERR reply may occur on any query, and access programs should be prepared for it. It has the form ERR : <code> : <string> :, for example ERR : NAMNFD : Name not found :.

The error code is a unique descriptor of at most 8 characters, which a program can use to handle the error automatically. The string is a message for programs that just want to log it. The defined codes are NAMNFD (name not in table), ADRNFD (address not in table), ILLCOM (command key not recognized) and TMPSYS (temporary system failure, try again later).
sections.eli5: If the librarian cannot find what you asked for, she says so with a short code and a sentence, so you know whether to try again later or give up.

items.label: Name not found
items.desc: The name is not in the table.

items.label: Address not found
items.desc: The address is not in the table.

items.label: Illegal command
items.desc: The command key was not recognized.
